newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia PM had "tea and toast" as emergency loomed.
newsitem.headline: Australia PM had "tea and toast" as emergency loomed.

text.p: As Australia's emergency services mobilised for the possible crash of Russia's Mars space probe carrying deadly plutonium, Prime Minister John Howard was breakfasting on tea and toast at his official residence, ignorant of the unfolfing drama, media reports said on Tuesday.

Howard, unaware of the potential disaster until told by U.S. President Bill Clinton two hours after Australian defence forces put themselves on alert on Monday, said he was angry at his officials' failure to warn him.
"The call to the Lodge (the prime minister's residence) came at 8.05 a.m., as Mr Howard was finishing his breakfast of tea and toast," The Australian newspaper said.
The Australian leader called a sudden news conference on Monday morning to announce the potential crisis and appeal for calm, saying he had mobilised the military and civil defence forces.

But emergency services within the defence department had gone on alert almost two hours earlier, without telling Howard, Defence Minister Ian McLachlan or armed forces chief General John Baker, the Herald Sun newspaper said.
Asked in a Tuesday radio interview if he was angry, Howard said: "If those claims are correct, and I don't want to say any more at this stage, I want to find out, but yes. In a word, yes, of course."
Defence officials admitted Howard and Defence Minister Ian McLachlan should have been told immeidately.
"(But) things were happening too fast for us to do that," defence official Rod McKinnon told the Herald Sun.
Officials said McLachlan had ordered a report on the incident and would make a statement in parliament later on Tuesday.
Forces remained on alert for several hours as U.S. scientists tracked the probe and tried to project where it would crash. Australian space-tracking facilities were unable to follow the craft.
But the six-tonne spacecraft eventually crashed harmlessly in a remote part of the Pacific Ocean, west of Chile, thousands of kilometres (miles) from Australia.
